Nourish
NUR-ish
v.
Old French norir, from Latin nutrire, to suckle, feed, rear—the root of nurse, nurture, and nutrition. To nourish is to feed a living thing toward growth, over time.

Biblical Definition

To nourish is to feed so as to sustain and grow, and Scripture uses it of bodies, households, churches and souls. God speaks of Israel as a father describing a raised child: I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me (Isa 1:2)—the tragedy is sharpened by the years of feeding that preceded the rebellion. Ruth's neighbors say of Obed that he shall be a nourisher of thine old age to Naomi, which is what covenant family does when the strength runs out at the far end of life. Paul's most weighted use is marital, and he argues from the body: no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church (Eph 5:29). A husband's duty toward his wife is set by two patterns at once—the automatic care every man gives his own body, and Christ's care of the church. Nourishing is therefore not romance and not provision only; it is the steady feeding of another life toward health. The pastoral form is Paul to Timothy: a good minister is one nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine (1 Tim 4:6). Note the passive—the minister is himself fed before he feeds anyone. Scripture also knows the counterfeit; James warns of men who have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter, feeding on the wages they withheld.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NOURISH as to feed and cause to grow; to supply with nutriment; to support; to maintain by feeding; and figuratively, to encourage, foster, or promote growth in.

expand to see more

NOURISH, v.t. — To feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste occasioned by the vital functions.

NOURISH, v.t. — To support; to maintain by feeding. Also, to encourage; to foster; to cherish; as, to nourish a hope, or to nourish rebellion. I have nourished and brought up children (Isa 1:2).

Key Scripture

Ephesians 5:29 — "For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church:"

1 Timothy 4:6 — "If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained."

Isaiah 1:2 — "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me."

Modern Corruption

Nourishment has been privatized as self-care and simultaneously cheapened into content—a man can feel well-fed on both and still be feeding no one, and be growing nothing that lasts.

expand to see more

The self-care vocabulary has annexed the language of feeding while removing its object. To nourish oneself is now a complete sentence, and the question of who else is being fed does not arise. Ephesians 5:29 uses self-nourishment as the assumed baseline—of course a man feeds his own body—and then makes it the measure of what he owes his wife. The instinct is not condemned; it is conscripted. A man who has learned to feed himself expertly and feeds no one else has taken the premise of the verse and refused its conclusion.

The second corruption is nutritional in the spiritual sense: volume mistaken for feeding. Clips, feeds, devotionals of a paragraph, sermons optimized for retention—a believer can consume religious material all day and remain unfed, because nourishing in Scripture is slow, repetitive, and aimed at growth rather than at stimulation. Paul's phrase is instructive: the minister is nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, passive and over time. Nobody grows on snacks, and no one can feed a church out of an empty pantry.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ektrephō, to nourish up or rear to maturity; Hebrew gadal, to make great or bring up—the verb of Isaiah's grieved fatherhood.

expand to see more

Greek ektrephō (G1625) — to nourish up, rear to maturity; used of a man's own flesh, of Christ and the church, and of fathers bringing up children (Eph 5:29; 6:4).

Greek entrephō (G1789) — to nourish in or train up in; nourished up in the words of faith (1 Tim 4:6).

Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to grow, become great, bring up; I have nourished and brought up children (Isa 1:2; 23:4; Dan 1:5).

Usage

"Nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church—the husband's standard, set twice."

"Nourished up in the words of faith—passive, and slow. The minister is fed before he feeds."

"Isaiah 1:2 — God as the father who fed the children who then rebelled."
